title: Efua and the Business That Almost Failed

pages.text: Ever since thirteen-year-old Efua refused to cut corners on her crunchy groundnut cakes, word of her honest quality had spread across town. Now two school canteens and the Saturday community football club wanted her nkate cakes! In one busy week, Efua and her grandmother Nana Ama roasted, wrapped and delivered a record one hundred packs at two cedis per pack.
sentences: Ever since thirteen-year-old Efua refused to cut corners on her crunchy groundnut cakes, word of her honest quality had spread across town.
Now two school canteens and the Saturday community football club wanted her nkate cakes!
In one busy week, Efua and her grandmother Nana Ama roasted, wrapped and delivered a record one hundred packs at two cedis per pack.
pages.alt: Efua and Nana Ama pack neat trays of golden groundnut cakes (nkate cake) in their clean kitchen.

pages.text: On Friday afternoon, Efua wrote in her notebook: One hundred packs times two cedis equals two hundred cedis! ‘Nana!’ Efua cheered, dancing around the veranda. ‘Last month we sold twenty packs a week, and now we have made two hundred cedis of profit! Our business is booming!’
sentences: On Friday afternoon, Efua wrote in her notebook: One hundred packs times two cedis equals two hundred cedis!
‘Nana!’ Efua cheered, dancing around the veranda.
‘Last month we sold twenty packs a week, and now we have made two hundred cedis of profit!
Our business is booming!’
pages.alt: Efua holds up her notebook happily on the veranda while Nana Ama watches with a gentle, knowing smile.

pages.text: Saturday morning arrived, and Efua walked to the market to buy groundnuts, sugar and wrappers for the new week’s orders from Auntie Dede. But when Efua opened her money tin at home before leaving, her smile vanished. Inside lay only a few notes, nowhere near two hundred cedis! Even worse, she needed one hundred and ten cedis just for raw ingredients, and she did not have enough cash in the tin!
sentences: Saturday morning arrived, and Efua walked to the market to buy groundnuts, sugar and wrappers for the new week’s orders from Auntie Dede.
But when Efua opened her money tin at home before leaving, her smile vanished.
Inside lay only a few notes, nowhere near two hundred cedis!
Even worse, she needed one hundred and ten cedis just for raw ingredients, and she did not have enough cash in the tin!
pages.alt: Efua stares in shock into her nearly empty metal cash tin on the kitchen table.

pages.text: ‘Did someone steal from my tin?’ Efua asked in panic. Nana Ama sat down beside her and opened a fresh ruled ledger book. ‘Nobody stole a pesewa, Efua. You have just discovered the most important lesson in business: high sales do not automatically mean high profit, and revenue is not the same as cash in your hand. Let us trace every cedi together.’
sentences: ‘Did someone steal from my tin?’ Efua asked in panic.
Nana Ama sat down beside her and opened a fresh ruled ledger book.
‘Nobody stole a pesewa, Efua.
You have just discovered the most important lesson in business: high sales do not automatically mean high profit, and revenue is not the same as cash in your hand.
Let us trace every cedi together.’
pages.alt: Nana Ama opens a clean ruled ledger book on the table beside Efua and her receipts.

pages.text: ‘First,’ said Nana Ama, ‘the two hundred cedis from selling one hundred packs at two cedis each is your revenue, the total sales price before any expenses are paid. Confusing revenue with profit is why many growing businesses fail! To find your true profit, we must subtract both your variable costs and your fixed costs.’
sentences: ‘First,’ said Nana Ama, ‘the two hundred cedis from selling one hundred packs at two cedis each is your revenue, the total sales price before any expenses are paid.
Confusing revenue with profit is why many growing businesses fail!
To find your true profit, we must subtract both your variable costs and your fixed costs.’
pages.alt: Efua writes the heading Revenue at the top of her ledger page while listening to Nana Ama.

pages.text: ‘Variable costs are expenses that go up with every pack you make,’ Nana Ama explained. ‘This week, groundnuts, sugar and clean wrappers cost one cedi and ten pesewas per pack. For one hundred packs, that was one hundred and ten cedis. Plus, when Wednesday’s heavy rainstorm flooded the footpath, you paid thirty cedis for a taxi so the school order would not get soaked. One hundred and ten plus thirty equals one hundred and forty cedis in variable costs.’
sentences: ‘Variable costs are expenses that go up with every pack you make,’ Nana Ama explained.
‘This week, groundnuts, sugar and clean wrappers cost one cedi and ten pesewas per pack.
For one hundred packs, that was one hundred and ten cedis.
Plus, when Wednesday’s heavy rainstorm flooded the footpath, you paid thirty cedis for a taxi so the school order would not get soaked.
One hundred and ten plus thirty equals one hundred and forty cedis in variable costs.’
pages.alt: Efua adds up her ingredient and rainy-day transport receipts on her calculator.

pages.text: ‘What are fixed costs?’ asked Efua. ‘Fixed costs are regular business expenses you must pay every week even if your sales go up or down,’ said Nana Ama. ‘This week you rented the Saturday stall table and contributed to our kitchen charcoal and electricity, which cost twenty-five cedis in total. Adding one hundred and forty cedis of variable costs and twenty-five cedis of fixed costs gives one hundred and sixty-five cedis in total expenses!’
sentences: ‘What are fixed costs?’ asked Efua.
‘Fixed costs are regular business expenses you must pay every week even if your sales go up or down,’ said Nana Ama.
‘This week you rented the Saturday stall table and contributed to our kitchen charcoal and electricity, which cost twenty-five cedis in total.
Adding one hundred and forty cedis of variable costs and twenty-five cedis of fixed costs gives one hundred and sixty-five cedis in total expenses!’
pages.alt: Nana Ama points to the two cost columns in the ledger as Efua totals 140 plus 25 to get 165 cedis.

pages.text: Efua subtracted one hundred and sixty-five cedis of total expenses from the two hundred cedis of revenue. ‘My actual profit for the week was thirty-five cedis, not two hundred!’ she gasped. ‘Wait, Nana, if I earned thirty-five cedis in profit, why does my tin have less cash than I need to buy next week’s groundnuts?’
sentences: Efua subtracted one hundred and sixty-five cedis of total expenses from the two hundred cedis of revenue.
‘My actual profit for the week was thirty-five cedis, not two hundred!’ she gasped.
‘Wait, Nana, if I earned thirty-five cedis in profit, why does my tin have less cash than I need to buy next week’s groundnuts?’
pages.alt: Efua looks puzzled as she compares her ledger profit of 35 cedis with the small amount of cash in her tin.

pages.text: At the market, Auntie Dede listened to Efua’s puzzle and nodded knowingly. ‘That is the difference between accounting profit and cash flow, Efua! Did every customer pay you in cash this week?’ Efua clapped her hand to her forehead. ‘No! The Hilltop School canteen took thirty packs worth sixty cedis on credit, promising to pay at the end of the month!’
sentences: At the market, Auntie Dede listened to Efua’s puzzle and nodded knowingly.
‘That is the difference between accounting profit and cash flow, Efua!
Did every customer pay you in cash this week?’ Efua clapped her hand to her forehead.
‘No!
The Hilltop School canteen took thirty packs worth sixty cedis on credit, promising to pay at the end of the month!’
pages.alt: At the market stall, Auntie Dede explains cash flow to Efua, who suddenly remembers the unpaid 60-cedi credit order.

pages.text: ‘Let us check your cash flow,’ said Auntie Dede. ‘Out of two hundred cedis in sales, sixty cedis is still sitting in the canteen’s pocket, so you only collected one hundred and forty cedis in actual cash. Yet you already paid out one hundred and sixty-five cedis in cash for ingredients, transport and stall rent! You had a twenty-five-cedi cash shortfall, plus you spent ten cedis on snacks when you thought you were rich!’
sentences: ‘Let us check your cash flow,’ said Auntie Dede.
‘Out of two hundred cedis in sales, sixty cedis is still sitting in the canteen’s pocket, so you only collected one hundred and forty cedis in actual cash.
Yet you already paid out one hundred and sixty-five cedis in cash for ingredients, transport and stall rent!
You had a twenty-five-cedi cash shortfall, plus you spent ten cedis on snacks when you thought you were rich!’
pages.alt: Auntie Dede uses three small bowls of groundnuts on her counter to show Cash In, Cash Out, and Unpaid Credit.

pages.text: On the way home, Efua’s classmate Kwabena rode by on his bicycle. ‘If costs are high, Efua, just put fewer groundnuts in each pack and print a fancy label saying Made with Pure Wild Honey even if it is plain sugar!’ Efua shook her head firmly. ‘Never, Kwabena. Dishonest marketing destroys trust. I will fix my business with real financial management, not lies.’
sentences: On the way home, Efua’s classmate Kwabena rode by on his bicycle.
‘If costs are high, Efua, just put fewer groundnuts in each pack and print a fancy label saying Made with Pure Wild Honey even if it is plain sugar!’ Efua shook her head firmly.
‘Never, Kwabena.
Dishonest marketing destroys trust.
I will fix my business with real financial management, not lies.’
pages.alt: Along the roadside, Kwabena leans on his bicycle suggesting a shortcut while Efua shakes her head firmly.

pages.text: With Auntie Dede’s advice, Efua made three smart changes: she required a fifty-percent cash deposit on all bulk canteen orders, joined Auntie Dede’s wholesale purchase to lower her ingredient cost to ninety pesewas per pack, and saved ten cedis every week in an emergency reserve fund for rainy days or sudden price rises. By month’s end, her ledger balanced and her business stood strong! The end.

By month’s end, her ledger balanced and her business stood strong!
The end.
pages.alt: Efua, Nana Ama and Auntie Dede smile together over a balanced ledger, a full cash box and a labelled emergency reserve jar.

activities.question: What is the difference between revenue and profit in Efua’s business?
options: Revenue is total sales (200 cedis); profit is what remains after costs
Revenue and profit mean the exact same thing
Profit is the money paid for taxi fares and charcoal
Revenue is only the money kept inside a bank account
activities.explanation: Revenue is total sales (100 × 2 = 200 cedis), whereas profit is Revenue minus all Variable and Fixed Costs.

activities.question: Efua had 200 cedis in revenue, 140 cedis in variable costs, and 25 cedis in fixed costs. What was her actual profit?
activities.explanation: Total expenses were 140 + 25 = 165 cedis; subtracting 165 from 200 cedis of revenue leaves 35 cedis of accounting profit.

activities.question: Why did Efua run short of cash to buy ingredients even though her business made a 35-cedi profit on paper?
options: 60 cedis was on unpaid credit, so cash in (140) was less than cash out (165)
She lost her money tin on the way to school
She gave away all 100 packs for free
activities.explanation: Selling 60 cedis on credit meant she only received 140 cedis in cash while paying 165 cedis in cash expenses, a cash-flow crunch!

glossary.definition: Total money received from selling goods or services before subtracting any expenses.
In business, variable costs are expenses like raw materials that change with the number of items produced.
In business, fixed costs are regular expenses like stall rent that stay the same each week regardless of sales volume.
An arrangement where a customer receives goods now and agrees to pay for them later.
Money saved and set aside by a business to handle unexpected emergencies or price increases.
